svg.desc: Map of Europe. Small blue dots are scattered inside each country, one dot per 199,000 people, 2,996 dots in total. The five countries the title names — Germany, the United Kingdom, France, Italy and Spain — carry the five biggest clouds of dots, each labelled directly on its own cluster: 1,646 of the 2,996 dots, more than half the map's population. Dots fall at random inside each country, so a tighter fill means more people per square kilometre rather than a bigger population — the tightest fills on this map are over Malta, Netherlands and Belgium, none of them among the five. That comparison holds along a latitude only: the projection draws the same density 4.3× more thinly at the top of the frame than at the bottom. Russia and seven micro-territories are not shown (see the caveat).
svg.text: More than half of this map's population lives in just five countries: Germany, the
United Kingdom, France, Italy and Spain.
Source: World Bank Open Data, indicator SP.POP.TOTL (population, total), 2023. · basemap © MapTiler, © OpenStreetMap
Shaded: the 42 countries counted in that total. Unshaded land is
outside this map — see the note below.
Russia is excluded: its population figure covers the whole transcontinental
country, but almost none of its territory falls inside this map's frame —
plotting its full population as dots confined to the small visible sliver near
Kaliningrad and St Petersburg would misrepresent both that sliver and the
true European picture. Seven micro-territories with no independent World
Bank population figure (Åland, Guernsey, Isle of Man, Jersey, Monaco, San
Marino, Vatican City) are also not shown. Each dot's position within its
country is random, not an address. Web Mercator stretches area with
latitude: one drawn square covers 4.3× more ground at 67°N than at 36°N,
so the same number of people per square kilometre is drawn 4.3× more
thinly in the north. Compare fills within a latitude, not up and down the
